version.rcText: A release candidate is a kernel that is not finished. Testing it helps Soplos find failures and make patches. It may not start.
version.noRustBinder: This kernel has no Rust Binder: it is built without Binder and without Rust, and Waydroid will not work with it.

revoke.title: Revoke your key?
revoke.text: No kernel or bootloader is signed with your key any more. You can remove the key from the firmware so that it no longer trusts it. The removal is confirmed on the blue screen at the next restart, with the password you set now.
revoke.done: The key is queued for removal. Restart the computer and confirm it on the blue screen.
revoke.error: The key could not be revoked

secureboot.description: Set up Secure Boot step by step so that your own kernels can start with it on.
secureboot.needKey: Create your key first, in the previous step.
secureboot.restartText: Save your work first. The computer restarts right away.

auto.title: Keep it signed
auto.text: When an update replaces a kernel or the bootloader, the new file has no signature of yours and the computer would not start with Secure Boot on. This signs them for you after every update.
auto.note: A copy of your key is kept in a folder that only the administrator can read.

status.title: Where things stand
status.notTrusted: The firmware does not trust it yet
status.notListed: The list could not be read

system.title: Your computer
system.setupOpen: Open: keys can be added without a signature (setup mode)
system.setupProtected: Protected: changes need a signature (user mode)

loaders.grub: Starts through shim. Shim trusts the key of Debian and, once enrolled, your key (MOK).
loaders.systemdBoot: Needs shim in front to use your key (MOK). Started directly, only the database of the firmware can trust it.
loaders.limine: Does not use shim: the firmware has to trust your certificate in its own database, and Limine checks the rest by hash.
loaders.payloadsTitle: Kernels and images on the boot partition
loaders.noPayloads: No kernels were found on the boot partition. systemd-boot loads them from there.
loaders.shimNote: If the firmware starts systemd-boot directly, your key has to be in the database of the firmware instead of in shim.

limine.title: Limine hardening
limine.text: Limine checks every file it loads by its hash, but only when the hash of its configuration is enrolled in its own binary. This works out the hashes, enrolls the configuration in a clean copy of Limine and signs it. Repeat it after each change of kernels or configuration; with automatic signing on, it is done for you.
limine.hashes: {matching} of {total} files have the right hash
limine.needTool: The limine tool is not installed.
limine.refresh: Update the hashes and enroll the configuration
limine.certText: Limine does not use shim, so the firmware has to trust your certificate in its own database. Copy it to the boot partition and add it from the firmware settings, usually under Secure Boot, Key Management, db, Append or Enroll.
limine.exportCert: Copy my certificate to the boot partition

chain.title: Would this computer start with Secure Boot on?
chain.shim: shim is next to the bootloader
chain.loader: The bootloader is signed by Debian or with your key
chain.kernels: Every kernel is signed by Debian or with your key
chain.autoSignOff: Updates are not signed automatically: turn it on in the signing step
chain.payloads: The kernels and images on the boot partition are trusted
chain.db: The firmware trusts your certificate in its own database
chain.enrolled: The configuration is enrolled in Limine
chain.hashes: Every file of limine.conf has the right hash
chain.yes: Yes: everything in the chain is trusted.
chain.no: Not yet: something in the chain would stop it. Fix what is marked above before turning Secure Boot on.

check.intro: Secure Boot is a feature of the firmware that only lets signed software start. The kernels you build, or get from outside, are not signed by anyone the firmware trusts. This guide creates your own key, tells the firmware to trust it and signs your kernels with it. The first steps are done only once.
check.legacy: This computer starts in legacy BIOS mode, where Secure Boot does not exist. You can ignore this guide.

key.text: The key has two halves. The private half signs your kernels and never leaves this computer. The public half is the one you give to the firmware.
key.needTools: Install the tools in the first step before.

enroll.text: The firmware has to be told to trust your key. You invent a password now and type it once, on a blue screen, when the computer restarts. This is done only once.
enroll.done: The firmware already trusts your key.
enroll.pendingTitle: The key is waiting for the restart. When the computer starts again:
enroll.blue1: On the blue screen choose Enroll MOK.
enroll.password: Invent a password of at least 8 characters. You need it once, at the restart.

dkms.text: Drivers that are built for each kernel, like the one of NVIDIA, are signed with a key of their own. The firmware has to trust it too, or they will not load with Secure Boot on.
dkms.done: The firmware already trusts the key of the drivers.
dkms.missing: There are driver modules, but their signing key is missing. Reinstall the driver from Soplos Welcome to create it.
dkms.sameScreen: It appears on the same blue screen as your key.

sign.text: A kernel has to be signed to start with Secure Boot on. The kernels you build here can be signed as part of the build. The ones that come from elsewhere, like XanMod or Liquorix, are signed here. The bootloader is signed too.
sign.bootloaderText: The bootloader starts the kernel, so the firmware has to trust it too. The one of Debian comes signed by Debian.
sign.needTools: Install the tools in the first step to see who signed each file.
sign.noBootloader: No bootloader was found on the boot partition.
sign.signLoader: Sign what is not trusted yet
sign.build: You can also sign a kernel when you build it.

enable.text: The last step is done in the firmware, not in this program.
enable.step1: Restart and open the firmware settings. Usually by pressing Del, F2, F10 or Esc while the computer starts.
enable.step2: Find the Secure Boot option, usually in the Security or Boot menu.
enable.step3: Set it to Enabled, save and exit.

password.tooShort: The password needs at least 8 characters.

advanced.title: Advanced
advanced.deleteText: Queues the removal of your key from the firmware and deletes it from this computer. The kernels signed with it will no longer start with Secure Boot on.
advanced.deleteEnrolled: The firmware trusts this key. It is queued for removal at the next restart, and you need a password to confirm it on the blue screen.
advanced.deleteLocal: The key never reached the firmware, so only its files on this computer are deleted.
advanced.resetText: Queues the removal of every key enrolled by hand, not only yours. Useful to clean old keys.
advanced.resetConfirm: Every key enrolled by hand is removed at the next restart, and you will have to enroll yours again. You need a password to confirm it on the blue screen.

batch.description: Build several kernels one after another.
batch.destRelative: The destination has to be a full path, like /home/you/kernels.
batch.revisionHint: 0 is a kernel version never built before. Raise it only when recompiling the same version with different patches (1 is the first recompile), so that apt sees a real upgrade.
batch.resume: Resume: skip the kernels already built in the destination
batch.allBuilt: Every selected kernel is already built in the destination.
batch.confirmText: {n} kernels of version {version} are built one after another and saved in {dest}. The sources are made again for every kernel.
batch.cancelText: The build in course is stopped and the queue ends. What was finished stays in the destination.
batch.busy: Another build is in course. Wait for it to end.
batch.failedText: {n} kernels were finished before it. The sources and the log of the one that failed are kept in {folder}.
